title: OpenAI Withdraws Three Math Papers as Navier-Stokes Proof Faces Verification Challenge
summary:
OpenAI has withdrawn three of the 722 mathematical manuscripts it released on Oct. 6 and revised 14 others. The collection, produced by an unreleased internal AI model, groups the work into 372 families of related results. OpenAI warned in its release documentation that some results without formal verification could contain errors.

A separate paper challenges the correspondence between OpenAI’s written Navier-Stokes proof and its formal verification in Lean, software that checks mathematical logic. Valerio Capraro, describing the paper’s findings, identified two mismatches: one written estimate requires four additional input derivatives, while its Lean counterpart requires five; a pressure-flux estimate uses a different bound and argument. Capraro wrote, “It is not clear whether these mismatches invalidate the entire proof.”

Researchers have also reported further improvements to OpenAI’s theoretical integer multiplication result. A contributor publishing as 0xdoug validated and merged Rohan’s contribution, reporting an exponent saving parameter of κ = 2⁻¹⁵, up from OpenAI’s original 2⁻¹⁸². The reported 2¹⁶⁷-fold increase concerns that parameter, not practical multiplication speed, and the submitted bound remains conditional on OpenAI’s algorithmic interfaces. The latest result combined techniques from several contributors.

selectedTweets.text:
The Association for Human Mathematics, on OpenAI's 722-paper release: "Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done."

It also urged mathematicians "to discontinue their work with OpenAI."

Fields Medalist Terence Tao reposted the statement on his blog as a guest post, and X has since run with it as Tao's own words. 

OpenAI has also withdrawn 3 of the papers, and 14 more have been revised since the release.

OpenAI's README on the drop did say that "some of the unformalized results could have issues. We will endeavor to fix any such issues quickly."

selectedTweets.text:
BREAKING: OpenAI’s solution to Navier–Stokes does not match its Lean verification.

The most important article to read today is not one of OpenAI’s 700 AI-generated math papers.

It is this other paper, making a deep and worrying point:

A Lean-verified proof does not automatically validate the proof written in natural language, nor does it mean that the formal statement captures the intended theorem.

During translation, an AI can change an assumption, weaken a statement, or replace the argument entirely.

It can hallucinate another theorem.

Lean correctly verifies the result.
But the proved result may no longer be what the paper claims.

This is a general problem. Things get spicy when the authors examine OpenAI’s proposed Navier–Stokes solution.

They identify at least two mismatches between the written intermediate results and their Lean counterparts:

One estimate claims that four additional input derivatives suffice. The Lean version requires five: a weaker result.

A pressure-flux estimate is obtained through a different bound, and proved through a different argument.

It is not clear whether these mismatches invalidate the entire proof.

But they raise an important issue.

OpenAI is flooding us with claimed revolutionary breakthroughs. Yet nobody knows whether the proofs are correct or whether they prove what they claim to be proving.

Epistemia at scale.
